title: Stop Telling Kids the World Is a Terrible Place
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Pondiscio challenges the school culture assumption that being real with children means confronting them with the harshness of the world. Drawing on Jeremy Clifton's research on primal world beliefs, he argues that believing the world is dangerous predicts worse life satisfaction and health, and that these beliefs shape experience rather than merely reflecting it. He then turns to schools, arguing that trauma-informed pedagogy, grim young adult reading lists, action civics and SEL's posture of fragility may be teaching pupils negative primals. He is careful to say suffering should not be denied and that the research is young. His closing proposal is that educators frame the world as basically safe, wondrous and alive while still naming specific dangers.
points: Clifton's research suggests primal world beliefs shape how people interpret experience, so teaching children that the world is bad may do lasting harm.
More than half of surveyed parents preferred dangerous-world beliefs for their children, mistakenly believing they would be better prepared for life.
Pondiscio sees trauma-informed pedagogy, dark young adult novels and action civics as tacitly modelling a broken-world view in schools.
He cautions that even the original ACE researchers say their metrics are being misused as de facto diagnostic tools in schools.
The proposed alternative is to name specific dangers while teaching that, on balance, the world is good and full of wonder.
quotes: Adults who care about children tend to believe it’s in their best interest to approach the world with caution. A naive or overly trusting child, we assume, is more likely to stumble into danger. So we try to instill a sense of wariness. Teachers and parents often pride themselves on being “real” with kids—helping them confront the harsh truths of poverty, racism, climate change, and other systemic challenges. We treat this as a mark of intellectual seriousness.

Crucially—and counter-intuitively—these beliefs are not simply shaped by life experience. In fact, Clifton’s research suggests the opposite: people’s primal beliefs tend to shape how they interpret their experiences. In one study, Clifton and his colleague Peter Meindl found that people’s primal beliefs—especially negative ones—strongly predicted lower life satisfaction, worse health, diminished flourishing, and even increased risk of suicide.

This insight should challenge many core assumptions of today’s education culture. From trauma-informed pedagogy to social justice curricula, many well-meaning educators have embraced a mission of radical truth-telling—foregrounding systemic injustice, historical oppression, and future threats in the name of equity and authenticity.
In one 2021 study, Clifton and Meindl found that 53 percent of parents preferred dangerous world beliefs for their children. They thought it would better prepare them for life.

Even our approach to civic education has shifted. The traditional study of government and history has given way to “action civics,” in which students are asked to identify and organize around real-world injustices. But this, too, risks reinforcing a negative primal: that the world is filled with problems and that one’s job as a citizen is to respond to crisis.

This question takes on greater urgency in the context of rising youth mental health challenges. After the pandemic, 75 percent of schools reported staff concerns about student depression and anxiety. SEL has been proposed as a solution, but it, too, often assumes a posture of psychological fragility and risk-aversion.

Rather, it suggests that the way we frame the world to children—especially in their formative years—can have a lifelong impact on their mental health, flourishing, and resilience. Children who grow up with positive primals don’t just feel better. They tend to do better.
